submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole is a token-level detector for a written message or record and for the act of carrying it to a recipient: it peaks (about 0.3 to 0.9 of max, well above the 0.25 active line) on the token that names a message, a kept record or its informational content - letter(s), note(s), memo(s), message(s), email(s), text, telegram, despatch/dispatch, correspondence, epistle, missive, reply, mail, envelope, stamp, document(s), file(s), sheet, log, dossier, report(s), statement, notice(s), reminder, notification, subpoena, memorandum, affidavit, warrant, certificate, papers, docs, documentation, instructions, information, data, source, footnote, appendix, graph - and on the verbs that bring such a thing to someone (send/sent/sends, mailed, forwarded, relayed, handed, brought/bring, conveyed, mail, showed/shown, wrote/write/written, inform(s/ed), report(ed), come/came/comes, return(ed)) and on the further-material tokens further, additional, extra and follow/follows/following/followed; the weaker members of the same family (page, record(s), form, invoice, figures, chart, summary, evidence, proof, ledger, transcript, delivered, transmitted, dispatched, told/tell, explained) clear the line only inside a sentence that also carries a strong one. The response is to the token form rather than to the sense of the sentence, so 'letter' fires equally in 'the letter of the law' and 'the letter B', 'Sentimental' fires on its ' Sent' piece, and a passage is predicted inactive when its only such-looking words are for published literary works (book, novel, poem, essay, article, paper, manuscript, draft, journal, magazine, newspaper, story, news, paragraph, advertisement, diary, chapter), bare information nouns (fact, content, question, answer, account, description, advice, insight, announcement), transaction slips (ticket, menu, schedule, label, receipt, bill, contract, licence, permit, petition, application, postcard, passport, visa, deed, charter, policy, agenda), generic handling or motion verbs (give, gave, pass, carry, take, go, went, open, keep, sell, move, receive, weigh) or public-speech and publishing verbs (announce, mention, state, declare, say, publish, print, quote, cite).

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The rain had not stopped for three days when Eliza finally left the house on the hill. The road below the orchard had turned to mud, and the wheels of the cart sank past their rims. Old Thomas walked ahead with a lantern, calling back over his shoulder whenever the horse stumbled. Nobody in the village remembered a spring so wet. The mill pond had risen until it touched the lower boards of the bridge, and the lane beyond the smithy ran like a brown river, carrying sticks and straw toward the sea.

She had spent the morning in the attic, sorting through what the family had left behind: a cracked mirror, a tin of buttons, three chairs with broken legs, and a trunk that had belonged to her grandmother. The mirror had been her mother's, and the buttons had been saved for a coat that was never sewn, though nobody could say for which child. The trunk smelled of cedar and dust, and there was a long scrape along one side where a strap had rubbed for fifty years.

She sat on the floor with her back against a beam and listened to the rain drum on the roof. The house had been quiet since the winter her grandmother died. Her cousins had promised to visit, and then the visits stopped. The orchard had been sold in pieces, the kitchen garden had gone to weeds, and the arguments about the debts had faded into a silence nobody wished to disturb. Eliza was back only to sort the rooms and sign whatever the solicitor put in front of her.

Near the bottom of the trunk, under a folded blanket, she found a bundle tied with string that crumbled at her touch. Inside lay a pressed flower, a child's shoe, and a ribbon the colour of dried blood. At the very bottom lay a letter, folded three times, its ink faded to a watery brown. It was addressed to a name she did not recognise and dated the summer before her grandmother was married.

She carried it down to the kitchen, where Thomas was drying his coat by the stove, and read it aloud. It spoke of a voyage, a debt repaid in secret, and a promise made to a woman who was not her grandmother. Thomas said only that the name belonged to a cousin nobody in the family spoke of, and that the rest of the bundle had been burned long ago. Eliza put the page in the drawer with the parish register, went back up the stairs, and watched the rain ease while a thin band of light opened above the orchard.

explanation_scores.explanation: The pole is a token-level detector for a written message or record and for the act of carrying it to a recipient: it peaks (about 0.3 to 0.9 of max, well above the 0.25 active line) on the token that names a message, a kept record or its informational content - letter(s), note(s), memo(s), message(s), email(s), text, telegram, despatch/dispatch, correspondence, epistle, missive, reply, mail, envelope, stamp, document(s), file(s), sheet, log, dossier, report(s), statement, notice(s), reminder, notification, subpoena, memorandum, affidavit, warrant, certificate, papers, docs, documentation, instructions, information, data, source, footnote, appendix, graph - and on the verbs that bring such a thing to someone (send/sent/sends, mailed, forwarded, relayed, handed, brought/bring, conveyed, mail, showed/shown, wrote/write/written, inform(s/ed), report(ed), come/came/comes, return(ed)) and on the further-material tokens further, additional, extra and follow/follows/following/followed; the weaker members of the same family (page, record(s), form, invoice, figures, chart, summary, evidence, proof, ledger, transcript, delivered, transmitted, dispatched, told/tell, explained) clear the line only inside a sentence that also carries a strong one. The response is to the token form rather than to the sense of the sentence, so 'letter' fires equally in 'the letter of the law' and 'the letter B', 'Sentimental' fires on its ' Sent' piece, and a passage is predicted inactive when its only such-looking words are for published literary works (book, novel, poem, essay, article, paper, manuscript, draft, journal, magazine, newspaper, story, news, paragraph, advertisement, diary, chapter), bare information nouns (fact, content, question, answer, account, description, advice, insight, announcement), transaction slips (ticket, menu, schedule, label, receipt, bill, contract, licence, permit, petition, application, postcard, passport, visa, deed, charter, policy, agenda), generic handling or motion verbs (give, gave, pass, carry, take, go, went, open, keep, sell, move, receive, weigh) or public-speech and publishing verbs (announce, mention, state, declare, say, publish, print, quote, cite).
